interface_detail: a JavaScript or WASM module; fetch handler, cron triggers, queue consumers
tooling: Wrangler; the runtime API; ctx.waitUntil for work after the response
chaining: the only free tier here that answers 100,000 HTTP requests a day and can hold a WebSocket
limits_note: there is no duration limit for an HTTP-triggered Worker while a user stays connected; cron and queue handlers are capped at 15 minutes

free_tier.stated: Workers Free: 100,000 requests a day, 10 ms of CPU time per request, 128 MB memory, 50 subrequests per request
free_tier.notes: no request-per-second cap; the free wall is CPU time and the daily request count

retention.stated: a Worker holds no disk; state lives in KV, D1, R2 or a Durable Object

egress.terms: response bodies are served from the edge with no per-byte charge stated on the limits page

limits.value: 50 subrequests per request on Free, 1,000 on Paid
6 simultaneous outgoing connections per request on both plans

identity_cost.detail: a Cloudflare account; no card for the Free plan

evidence.proved: Free: 100,000 requests a day, 10 ms CPU, 128 MB memory, 50 subrequests, 6 simultaneous outgoing connections
there is no hard duration limit for HTTP-triggered Workers; cron triggers and queue consumers are capped at 15 minutes
Paid raises CPU time to 5 minutes and subrequests to 1,000 per request

notes: 10 ms of CPU is the wall, not the 100,000 requests. A Worker can hold a connection open for hours and stream a response, which is why this is the only free runtime here that can serve. It cannot run a shell.

session_cap.note: no duration limit while a user is connected; 10 ms of CPU per request on Free

keep_rate.basis: an isolate is not billed between requests

persistent_storage.price_gib_month: R2 and D1 are separate products

network_out.ports: HTTP and WebSocket through the edge

extras.price_arithmetic: free at 100,000 requests a day; Paid is USD 5 a month with no request cap

binding_note: 10 ms of CPU per request is the wall: the 100,000-request allowance is generous and a JSON parse meets the CPU limit in the first request
